summary: Matthew 6 continues the Sermon on the Mount, teaching how to practice righteousness sincerely rather than for show. Jesus takes up three pillars of piety in turn—almsgiving, prayer, and fasting—and warns against doing them "before men, to be seen of them." The hypocrites who parade their giving, pray on street corners, and disfigure their faces already "have their reward"; but the disciple gives in secret, prays behind a shut door, and fasts unnoticed, trusting the Father "which seeth in secret" to reward openly. Against "vain repetitions," Jesus gives the model prayer: "Our Father which art in heaven," hallowing God's name, seeking His kingdom and will, asking daily bread, forgiveness of debts as we forgive, and deliverance from evil. He stresses that our own forgiveness of others conditions the Father's forgiveness of us. The chapter then turns to treasure and trust: lay up treasure in heaven, not on earth, "for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." The eye must be single, and no one can serve both God and mammon. Finally Jesus commands freedom from anxiety—consider the birds and the lilies, whom the Father feeds and clothes—and issues the great summons: "Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you," taking no anxious thought for tomorrow.
takeaways: Righteous deeds—almsgiving, prayer, and fasting—are to be done for God, not for human applause; the one who seeks the praise of men "have their reward" already, while the Father who sees in secret rewards openly.

The Lord's Prayer models right prayer: it begins with God's name, kingdom, and will before petitions for bread, forgiveness, and deliverance, and it deliberately avoids the "vain repetitions" of those who trust in "much speaking."
Forgiveness is reciprocal in this chapter: "if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you," but withholding forgiveness withholds it from oneself.
Where your treasure is, there your heart follows—so treasure is to be laid up in heaven, and "ye cannot serve God and mammon"; divided loyalty is no loyalty at all.

Anxiety is answered by providence and priority: the Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, so disciples are freed from anxious care by seeking "first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness."

crossRefs.label: Luke 11:2-4 — Luke's form of the Lord's Prayer
crossRefs.why: Luke preserves a shorter version of the same model prayer, given in a different setting when a disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray. The parallel shows the prayer as a fixed pattern of Jesus' own teaching rather than a one-time saying, and lets the two forms illuminate each other.

crossRefs.label: Luke 12:22-34 — do not be anxious; seek the kingdom
crossRefs.why: Luke gives a close parallel to the teaching on the ravens, the lilies, and treasure in heaven, climaxing in "seek ye the kingdom of God." The correspondence confirms this cluster of sayings on anxiety and providence as a coherent, remembered teaching of Jesus.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 58 — true fasting and hidden almsgiving
crossRefs.why: Isaiah contrasts outward fasting that seeks notice with the fast God chooses—loosing bonds and feeding the hungry. This prophetic critique of performative piety is the Old Testament background for Jesus' insistence that fasting and alms be directed to God, not display.

crossRefs.label: James 5:1-3 — riches that rust and moth-eaten garments
crossRefs.why: James echoes Jesus' warning about earthly treasure that moth and rust corrupt, applying it to the hoarding rich. The connection shows the apostolic church carrying forward Jesus' teaching on treasure and the heart into concrete moral exhortation.
